summary:
Project Canopus is an interactive, SI-powered dashboard over NASA's microgravity combustion data. Instead of predicting fires, it shows how close a fire-safety scenario is to what NASA has actually tested, and states what nobody has tested yet.

An engineer sets oxygen, pressure, airflow, fuel and a safety goal, or picks a mission preset such as a lunar base or a pressurized rover. Canopus ranks 17 NASA PSI investigations with a transparent score, shows the nearest of 1,425 tests, and charts the scenario against tested ranges and real mission atmospheres. The SI then explains what is known, what is unknown and what follows, citing a test, a study or a paper page for every claim.

This matters because a confident guess about an untested oxygen-pressure regime is dangerous. We checked the SI's answers statement by statement against the source tables and papers. Canopus turns scattered data into evidence an engineer can check.
details:
1. Project Name

Project Canopus

---

2. High-Level Project Summary

What we created:

Project Canopus is an interactive, SI-powered web dashboard over NASA's microgravity combustion data. It does not predict fires. It shows how far your scenario is from what NASA has actually tested, and it always says what nobody has tested yet.

The user sets a scenario: oxygen percentage, pressure, airflow, fuel and material, and a safety goal (prevention, smoke detection or suppression), or starts from one of five mission presets (ISS, Lunar Base, Rover, Spacesuit, Earth). The dashboard then:

- ranks 17 NASA PSI investigations by relevance with a transparent 0-100 score;

- shows the nearest individual tests out of 1,425, each with its result or measured values;

- draws the scenario against the tested ranges of each study, on an Oxygen-vs-Pressure coverage map, and against the atmospheres of real missions;

- opens any investigation as a page with NASA's own description, its papers and a chart of its tests;

- explains the scenario through the SI in three blocks: what is known, what is unknown, and what follows, with a source under every claim, plus a follow-up chat.

Users can also add their own study from a CSV table, and export the nearest tests as CSV.

The problem we are solving:

NASA's archive of low-gravity combustion experiments is large, scattered across tables and papers, and hard to compare. An engineer planning fire safety for a lunar habitat or a pressurized rover needs to know quickly which experiments apply to their conditions, how close those experiments really are, and where the evidence stops.

How our project aligns with the challenge:

The challenge asks for a dashboard that summarizes, ranks and interprets combustion investigations. Canopus summarizes each investigation (NASA's objectives and approach, test tables turned into charts), ranks them against a concrete fire-safety need, and interprets the result with Super Intelligence (SI) that is bound to the data: it may only use numbers and sources the system gives it.

Why our solution matters:

In combustion, a confident guess about an untested oxygen-pressure regime is dangerous. Canopus keeps the evidence and its limits visible at the same time. We checked the SI's answers statement by statement against the source tables and papers. That makes the tool something an engineer can check, not just read.

5. Detailed project description

0. The story of Project Canopus

In January 1967 the Apollo 1 crew died when fire broke out in their oxygen-filled cabin during a ground test. Thirty years later a fire from an oxygen generator burned aboard the Mir space station while the crew fought it in a module filling with smoke. And during Artemis II a smoke alarm went off far from home; as the commander put it, "[If] you want to get somebody's attention really quick, make the fire alarm go off in your spacecraft when you're still about 80,000 miles from home." Fire is the hazard that spaceflight has never been able to engineer away.

Our team is six first-year university students: a backend lead with several years of production coding experience, three physics and mathematics specialists, a design-focused developer, and a full-stack programmer. When we reviewed the NASA Space Apps challenges we did not arrive with a ready-made pitch. We chose "Flame in Freefall" because it looked like the hardest, most intellectually demanding puzzle on the list.

Once we read the challenge closely, the problem clicked for both the scientists and the engineers in the group. Future lunar habitats and pressurized rovers will use higher-oxygen, lower-pressure atmospheres (30%+ O2 at 10.2 psi or less), materials are much more flammable there, and PSI holds no true partial-gravity combustion data until experiments such as LUCI and FM2 report. A chatbot that smoothly guesses an answer for an untested regime is worse than useless here: it is dangerous.

That realization shaped every technical decision. Our physics teammates insisted on seeing the exact boundaries of experimental coverage, which led to the coverage map and the chart of tested ranges. Our developers built a lightweight, verifiable pipeline: a deterministic relevance score, keyword search over NASA papers, and SI explanations that must cite a test, a study or a page for every claim and must list what is unknown.

1. What the Project Does

- Scenario input: oxygen, pressure, airflow, fuel phase, material and goal, or one of five mission presets. Everything recalculates as the sliders move.

- Ranking: every investigation gets a score from 0 to 100 (goal match 30, fuel 25, oxygen 20, pressure 15, airflow 10). Nothing is hidden; weak matches simply rank lower.

- Nearest tests: the ten tests closest to the scenario, with their result. Where NASA's table has no burned / went-out result, the dashboard shows what the test measured instead (smoke aging, gas composition, fuel rate), and says so.

- Comparison of conditions: for the chosen studies, bars show the tested range of oxygen, pressure and airflow and a line marks the scenario, so a gap is visible at a glance.

- Coverage map: all tests on an Oxygen-vs-Pressure plane, coloured by result, with the scenario marked.

- Atmospheres: total pressure and oxygen share for Earth, the ISS, a lunar base, a spacesuit and the user's scenario.

- Study pages: NASA's objectives, approach and hypothesis for each investigation, its papers with links, the full test table, and a chart where the engineer chooses the axes.

- SI interpretation and chat: known / unknown / implications with clickable sources, and follow-up questions on the same data.

- Add study: upload a CSV with a name and description; the SI matches unfamiliar column names and units, and the study joins the ranking.

2. How It Works

- Data in memory: investigation cards, materials, NASA test tables (CSV) and papers (PDF) live in the data/ folder and are loaded at server start. There is no database.

- Ranking and distances: the backend (FastAPI, pandas) scores each investigation and measures how far every test is from the scenario in oxygen, pressure and airflow.

2.1. How the SI works

The SI never answers from its own memory. For every question the server assembles a package of evidence and hands it to the model together with strict rules. The model's job is to read that package and explain it; it does not compute scores, distances or statistics.

What the model receives for each scenario:

- The scenario itself: oxygen, pressure, airflow, fuel, material and goal.

- The five top-ranked investigations: their score and how it was earned, the tested ranges of oxygen, pressure and airflow, fuels and samples, what was varied and measured, NASA's own description of how the investigation was run, the count of each test result in its table, and our documented assumptions (for example, ISS cabin pressure where the table gives none).

- The ten nearest test rows straight from the NASA tables: test ID, fuel, oxygen, pressure, airflow, diluent (CO2, helium), result and measured values such as burn time or final gas composition.

- Up to five more tests that do have a recorded result, even if they are not among the ten nearest, so the model cannot claim "no results exist" when they do.

- Six excerpts from NASA papers found by retrieval (RAG), each with its file name and page number.

Retrieval (RAG):

- 24 NASA papers and reports are split into 1,128 overlapping passages (220 words, 40-word overlap); each passage keeps its file and page.

- Search is BM25 keyword ranking (rank-bm25). We chose it over vector embeddings because it is deterministic, needs no extra model or database, and exact technical terms (PMMA, Halon, psi) matter here.

- Three separate queries run for every scenario, two passages each: one about the mission environment (for a rover: lunar gravity, partial gravity), one about the scenario topic (goal, fuel, conditions), one about the top-ranked investigations. No more than two passages come from the same paper. A single combined query kept returning the same pages for every scenario; three queries fixed that.

- In the chat, four more passages are retrieved by the user's question itself.

The system prompt:

A specialized prompt of 23 rules turns the model into a cautious analyst. The main ones:

- use only numbers, test IDs and facts from the package; never invent or recalculate;

- answer in three lists: known, unknown, implications; every "known" and "implication" item must cite a test, an investigation or a paper page;

- the first "known" item states plainly how well the scenario is covered;

- for lunar scenarios, say that the tests provided were run in microgravity or normal gravity, and cite partial-gravity papers only with their limits;

- a missing column means "not recorded in the PSI summary table", not "did not happen"; assumed values are called assumptions;

- a conclusion must follow from the fact it cites; no general safety advice;

- keep the direction of every finding exact (minimum vs maximum, higher vs lower);

- definitions the model would otherwise guess: what the FLEX outcomes Extinction, Completion and Disruption mean, what the flammability map shows, how airflow was recorded in each table.

Most of these rules were added after our team read the answers against the sources and found a specific mistake.

Structured output and checks:

- The answer must fit a fixed schema (three lists of items, each with text and typed sources). An answer whose "known" or "implication" item has no source is rejected.

- After each answer the server checks in code that every cited test, investigation and page was really in the package, and that the numbers in the text appear in it.

- For lunar presets a statement about the missing partial-gravity data is guaranteed even if the model omits it.

Other uses of the SI:

- Follow-up chat: the same package plus the earlier interpretation and the conversation; sources are written inline and become clickable.

- Adding a study: when a user uploads a table with unfamiliar column names or units, the model maps the columns (oxygen, pressure, airflow, fuel, result) and the server converts units; the user sees which columns were matched.

Models and speed:

- Claude (Anthropic SDK), Gemini (google-genai) or any OpenAI-compatible service, including local servers such as Ollama or LM Studio; the provider, model and key can be chosen in Settings and the key stays in the user's browser.

- Explanations for the five presets are pre-generated and served instantly; other scenarios are answered live in about half a minute.

3. Advantages & Key Benefits

- Evidence, not prediction: the tool reports the nearest confirmed experiments and how far they are, and never extrapolates a result.

- Gaps are part of the answer: every interpretation has an "unknown" block, and the absence of partial-gravity data is stated for lunar scenarios.

- Checked by people and by code: our team checked the SI's answers against the sources, and each answer is verified against its inputs.

- Transparent ranking: the score is a published formula, so anyone can see why a study ranks where it does.

- Open to new data: a new table can be added from the interface in a minute.

- Lightweight: no database and no GPU; runs on a laptop. Works with cloud or self-hosted models.

- Custom interface: charts are hand-built SVG, with React 19, Vite 6, light and dark themes.

4. Goals & Objectives

Turn scattered combustion data into a decision-support tool that an aerospace engineer, researcher or student can trust: find the investigations that apply to a fire-safety scenario, see exactly how well it is covered, and understand the limits of the evidence before making a design decision.

5. Future Prospects

5.1. Ready for lunar and Martian gravity data

New partial-gravity results from LUCI (Lunar-g Combustion Investigation) and FM2 (Flammability of Materials on the Moon) can be added through the same "add study" flow the moment they are published, and compared with the microgravity and normal-gravity results already there.

5.2. Physics-informed uncertainty

Use microgravity and 1g results as bounds for intermediate gravity, together with partial-gravity mimics such as ACME's E-FIELD Flames, to mark high-uncertainty zones on the coverage map, for example the oxygen-rich atmospheres of lunar rovers.

5.3. Recommendations and mission playbooks

Let the SI propose which material or test condition to check next, and turn exported evidence into structured safety notes for mission planners.

5.4. Fire safety on Earth

The same workflow can serve terrestrial fire engineering: firefighter protective gear, confined spaces in aviation and submarines, and clean suppression such as fine water mist.

6. Technology Stack & Environment

- Programming languages:

- Python 3 (backend, tested locally on Python 3.14)

- TypeScript and CSS (frontend)

- Hardware:

- Any laptop or small server; no GPU needed for the app itself.

- Backend:

- FastAPI on uvicorn, Pydantic, python-dotenv

- pandas (test tables), pypdf (papers)

- rank-bm25 (keyword search for retrieval-augmented generation over NASA papers)

- Anthropic SDK (Claude), google-genai (Gemini), openai SDK with instructor for structured answers from Gemini and OpenAI-compatible models

- pytest (21 tests)

- Frontend:

- React 19, Vite 6

- Plain CSS with variables, light and dark themes, IBM Plex Mono

- Hand-built SVG charts (no chart library), @paper-design/shaders-react for the animated landing page

- Data and storage:

- JSON (investigation cards, materials, ready answers), CSV (NASA test tables), PDF (papers). No relational or vector database. User settings and conversations stay in the browser.

- AI techniques:

- Retrieval-augmented generation (BM25, three queries per scenario, page-level citations)

- Specialized system prompt (23 grounding rules) and schema-enforced structured output

- Automatic grounding checks of sources and numbers; pre-generated answers for the presets

- External services:

- Model API (Claude, Gemini or an OpenAI-compatible endpoint)

- Google Fonts

8. AI

AI inside the product (the SI)

A large language model (Claude by Anthropic by default; Gemini or any OpenAI-compatible model, including local ones, can be selected in Settings) does three jobs: it writes the scenario interpretation, answers follow-up questions in the chat, and matches column names when a user uploads a table.

How it is used:

- Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): the model answers from retrieved evidence, not from memory. For each scenario the server retrieves six passages from 24 NASA papers (1,128 passages, BM25 keyword search with rank-bm25, three separate queries for the mission environment, the scenario topic and the top-ranked investigations) and attaches the file and page of each.

- Structured evidence from the tables: together with the passages the model gets the ranking, the tested ranges and NASA descriptions of the top five investigations, the ten nearest test rows with their results and measured values, and the nearest tests that have a recorded result.

- Specialized system prompt: 23 rules that keep the model to the given numbers and sources, require an "unknown" block, forbid treating a missing table column as "did not happen", label assumed values as assumptions, and define domain terms it would otherwise guess (FLEX outcomes, the flammability map).

- Structured output: the answer must fit a fixed schema of known / unknown / implications, where each item carries typed sources (test, investigation, paper page); items without a source are rejected.

- Grounding checks in code: after each answer the server verifies that every cited test, investigation and page was in the evidence, and that the numbers in the text appear there.

- Division of labour: the relevance score, distances, coverage map and charts are computed by ordinary code. The model explains; it does not calculate.

- Column mapping for uploads: the model maps unfamiliar column names and units to oxygen, pressure, airflow, fuel and result; the server does the unit conversion and shows the user what was matched.

- Pre-generated answers: interpretations for the five mission presets are generated in advance and served instantly.

Details are in section 5, part 2.1 "How the SI works".

AI tools used during development

We used Claude (Claude Code), Gemini (AI Studio) and GitHub Copilot (VS Code agent) to:

- generate and review code,

- help us interpret the challenge,

- find and collect NASA papers,

- translate and condense NASA's investigation descriptions,

- prepare the 7-slide presentation,

- help write this description.

The SI's answers shown in the demo were checked by our team against the source tables and papers.
